title: Thiamethoxam‐Induced Haematobiochemical Alterations and Gonadal Damage in Banded Gourami, Trichogaster fasciata
content:
ABSTRACT

Thiamethoxam (THM), a systemic neonicotinoid insecticide extensively used in modern agriculture, has raised growing environmental concerns owing to its persistence and frequent occurrence in aquatic ecosystems. Here, we evaluated the chronic haematological, cytogenetic and gonadal histopathological toxicity of THM exposure (9.37–150 mg/L) in banded gourami (Trichogaster fasciata) across 30, 60 and 90 days. The results demonstrated a significant increase in glucose and white blood cell (WBC) levels, accompanied by significant decreases in haemoglobin, red blood cell (RBC) count and packed cell volume (PCV) in a time and concentration dependent manner. Cytogenetic assessment revealed concentration-dependent increases in erythrocytic nuclear abnormalities (ENAs), including micronuclei, binucleated, notched nuclei, nuclear buds and nuclear bridges, as well as cellular abnormalities such as elongated, twin, teardrop, fusion and spindle-shaped cells, confirming THM-induced genotoxic and cytotoxic effects. Semi-quantitative histopathological analysis of reproductive tissues showed pronounced ovarian lesions exposed to THM, including adhesion (AD), expansion of interfollicular spaces (IFS), degeneration of ovigerous lamellae (DOL), necrosis (NE), degenerated perinuclear oocytes (DPNO), cytoplasmic clumping (CC) and cytoplasmic retraction (CR). Testicular alterations included empty lumens (EL), damaged Sertoli cells (DSC), irregular seminiferous tubules (ISST), breakage of seminiferous tubules (BST) and degeneration of interstitial Leydig cells (DICL). These integrated biomarker responses demonstrate that prolonged THM exposure impairs hematopoietic integrity and disrupts reproductive physiology of banded gourami. The findings underscore the ecological risks associated with THM contamination and highlight the urgent need for stricter regulatory monitoring to protect aquatic biodiversity.
